target.title: Plantinga and Ash‘arites on Divine Simplicity
target.thesis: The objection that no distinction can be drawn within God, so that divine attributes cannot be distinguished from God's essence, is inconsistent with the doctrine of divine simplicity, and the reductio arguments against simplicity (Plantinga, Baghdādī, Taftāzānī) rest on a mistaken presumption of such a distinction.

W3115675310.arg1.r1.text: Divine simplicity, as the argument uses it, requires that every divine attribute be identical with the divine essence, with no real distinction between God's essence and any uncreated energies through which attributes are predicated.

W3115675310.arg1.r2.text: The doctrine rejected is the identity-version of divine simplicity, on which every divine attribute is identical with the essence; the conclusion is restricted accordingly, and positions distinguishing essence from uncreated energies are not claimed to fall under the reductio.

objections.text: Consider Ruth, a Trappist-style contemplative who holds that God is simple and also a personal agent who hears prayers. She prays for rain during a drought in Almería. On the argument's reading, c006 says divine simplicity makes God an abstract object because properties are abstract objects. But Ruth's case shows the inference fails: the step needs the premise that God is a property, and nothing in the doctrine requires that. Simplicity says God has no composition of essence and existence, or of substance and attributes. It does not say God is identical with a property such as 'being omnipotent.' Ruth can hold that the divine essence is a concrete, intelligent, willing subject whose simple nature is what grounds its acts of hearing and answering. Her view keeps God personal and simple, so simplicity does not entail abstractness.
objections.premise_fails_because: c006 assumes God must be a property, but divine simplicity only requires the absence of metaphysical composition in God, which is compatible with God being a concrete personal agent rather than an abstract object.

objections.text: In the video game Apex, the final boss's hit points, attack power, and speed are all coded as the exact same integer, 999, and are not distinct variables—each attribute just is that core value. On the stat screen, however, players see three separate bars labeled HP, ATK, and SPD. The designers do not call this one attribute; they treat it as three distinct attributes that share one identical ground. The players plan around three different abilities. Therefore, even when attributes are strictly identical in their underlying reality, it does not follow that there is only one attribute.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.c004 fails because attributes that are identical at their ground can still be multiple distinct attributes in the operative sense, as when one integer supports three separate game stats.

objections.text: Sister Clara, a Thomist theologian, accepts divine simplicity: God has no composition; God's essence is God himself. She affirms that 'God is omnipotent,' 'God is omniscient,' and 'God is omnibenevolent' are each true. But she holds these are genuinely distinct attributes: each captures a different aspect of the one divine reality under a different intelligible characterization. Swapping 'omnipotent' for 'omniscient' changes a sentence's meaning. For Clara, divine simplicity means no attribute exists as a constituent separate from God's essence—there is one simple divine being, not a bundle of properties. But the attributes, as predicative concepts, remain formally distinct: really united in the one essence, yet not identical to each other. The premise assumes divine simplicity forces strict identity among attributes, but Clara's coherent position shows divine simplicity is compatible with real unity of attributes in the essence alongside formal multiplicity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c003 fails because it assumes divine simplicity entails strict, transitive identity among all attributes, but a coherent defender can hold that attributes are really united in one simple essence while remaining formally distinct as predicative characterizations.

objections.text: Consider a being whose essence is perfectly unified yet manifests distinct, non-identical attributes—like a single light source that is simultaneously bright, warm, and white. Here, brightness, warmth, and color are distinct properties of the light, yet all are identical to the light itself. An observer can meaningfully distinguish these attributes without them collapsing into one, even though each is identical to the source. The attributes are multiple in description and effect, yet one in origin.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c005 fails because distinct attributes can be identical to a single essence without being identical to each other.

objections.text: Consider a blacksmith whose entire being is one undivided act of shaping iron. Her strength, skill, and intention are not separable parts but one unified, concrete activity. She is a personal agent who creates, wills, and acts in the world. She is not an abstract object. Now suppose divine simplicity collapses omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence into one undivided essence. The premise says this forces God to be abstract, since properties are abstract objects. But the blacksmith's unified act is not a property; it is a concrete agent's activity. Simplicity (having no proper parts) does not entail abstractness. A single undivided concrete substance that wills, acts, and creates is not an abstract object merely because its attributes are not numerically distinct. The premise equivocates: it treats 'being a property' as equivalent to 'being an abstract object,' then slides from 'no multiplicity of parts' to 'therefore abstract,' as though unity of essence necessarily strips concrete agency. The blacksmith shows unity of nature does not dissolve personal causation.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c006 fails because it equivocates between 'having no proper parts' and 'being an abstract object'; a concrete, unified, personal agent can be simple in essence while still acting and creating, so divine simplicity does not force God into abstractness.

objections.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who believes divine simplicity is false but still worthy of consideration due to its historical significance and the potential for new insights. Emma's intention is to understand the concept better, not to reject it outright. In her research, she encounters various interpretations of divine simplicity, some of which seem more plausible than others. Emma's belief that divine simplicity is false does not automatically lead her to reject it, as she values the intellectual exercise of exploring its implications.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that considering divine simplicity as false necessarily means rejecting it, which is not the case for individuals like Emma who approach the concept with a more nuanced perspective.

objections.text: Father Thomas, a Thomist priest, teaches that God’s essence is simple: it is actus essendi, a concrete participation in being, not a collection of abstract properties. In his parish, a believer asks why God can love and create personally if simplicity makes Him an abstract object. Thomas explains that simplicity affirms God’s unity of act, not His lack of personality: the same simple essence is the source of divine love, power, and knowledge. When the believer prays, she experiences God’s personal response, confirming that God operates as a personal creator, not as a detached abstract. This lived example shows that divine simplicity does not entail God’s abstractness, contradicting premise c006.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c006 fails because Thomist classical theism holds that divine simplicity denotes a simple, concrete essence, preserving God’s personal creator nature, not making Him an abstract object.

objections.text: A saint participates in the uncreated light of God. This light is not the unknowable essence of God, yet it is truly God. God is simple in His essence, but He communicates Himself through distinct, uncreated energies. When we speak of His love, His justice, or His power, we are describing these divine energies. These energies are distinct from the essence, yet they are not separate from God. They provide multiplicity in how God acts and is known without compromising His essential unity. Divine attributes correspond to these energies rather than the essence itself, preserving both simplicity and the reality of distinct divine properties.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c003 fails because divine simplicity does not necessitate that all attributes are identical to the essence, as God possesses distinct, uncreated energies.

objections.text: A scholar believes that a single entity can be described using multiple distinct terms without those terms implying the existence of multiple entities. For instance, one individual can be described as both a 'father' and a 'doctor.' While these descriptions are conceptually different, they both refer to the same underlying person. Similarly, 'omnipotence' and 'omniscience' can be distinct ways for humans to conceptualize the one divine essence. The ability to use different words to describe God does not necessitate that the attributes are ontologically separate. Therefore, c005 fails because it assumes that the conceptual plurality of attributes necessitates an ontological plurality.
objections.premise_fails_because: c005 fails because it assumes that the conceptual plurality of attributes necessitates an ontological plurality.

objections.text: Consider Maren, a theology student who holds that God is simple, and her teacher Oren, who holds that God's essence is one but that God's goodness is expressed to creatures through uncreated energies. Maren asks: does simplicity require that the energies be identical with the essence? Oren replies that his view has a real distinction between essence and energies, yet still treats God as simple in the sense that no compositional parts exist in God. Suppose the lab's premise r1 is true: simplicity requires identity of every attribute with the essence, with no real distinction from any uncreated energies. Then Oren's position, which the argument calls a version of simplicity, is counted as simplicity while denying the required identity. The premise is therefore being used to define simplicity in a way that excludes a position that many who hold simplicity accept, so the inference from r1 to the conclusion targets a stipulated doctrine rather than the doctrine people actually hold. Because r1 smuggles in the identity thesis as part of the definition, the argument's rejection step applies to a doctrine that Oren, holding simplicity while distinguishing energies, does not hold.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r1 fails because it defines divine simplicity as requiring identity of all attributes with the essence plus denial of any real distinction from uncreated energies, which Oren's coherent view of simplicity with a real essence-energies distinction contradicts, showing that r1 builds a contested identity thesis into the definition rather than stating what simplicity requires.

objections.text: A graduate student named Sam presents the argument, adding arg1.r2 because he intends to spare his Orthodox friend, Sister Maria, who distinguishes God’s simple essence from his multiple uncreated energies. Maria believes God is a concrete personal creator whose essence is simple but whose energies—love, power, wisdom—are genuinely distinct from it. During the Q&A, another student invokes c006 against Maria: if divine simplicity makes God an abstract object because properties are abstract, then since Maria still identifies God with the simple essence, her God is an abstract object too. Sam tries to block this by citing arg1.r2, but the audience sees that c006’s reasoning—that a simple essence is property-like and therefore abstract—applies regardless of whether energies are distinguished. Maria’s concrete-creator God is still swallowed by the reductio.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.arg1.r2 fails because its carve-out for essence-energy views collapses once c006’s implication that a simple essence is an abstract object is applied to anyone who identifies God with that essence, including those who distinguish essence from energies.

objections.text: Consider a geometer who attributes to a triangle both 'being trilateral' (having three sides) and 'being triangular' (having three angles). These have distinct senses: one concerns sides, the other angles. They also have distinct predicative roles: 'is trilateral' and 'is triangular' feature in different proofs and explanations. Yet every competent geometer treats these as a single attribute of the figure, not two coextensive but distinct attributes. When a student asks how many attributes the triangle has, the answer is not inflated to two merely because two descriptions with different senses apply. The distinct senses and predicative roles do not individuate distinct attributes here; ontological identity settles the count. The geometer's practice directly contradicts the claim that senses or predicative roles, rather than ontological identity, individuate attributes. If distinct senses sufficed for distinct attributes, the triangle would have arbitrarily many attributes—one for every equivalent characterization— which is absurd.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.arg1.r3 fails because 'trilateral' and 'triangular' have distinct senses and predicative roles yet constitute a single attribute, showing that senses do not individuate attributes when ontological identity is present.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection to c006 holds that the inference from divine simplicity to God's being an abstract object is invalid: it needs the further premise that God is identical with a property, such as being omnipotent, which simplicity does not entail. Simplicity denies only compositional distinctions (essence/existence, substance/accident), so God can be a simple, concrete, intelligent and willing subject who hears and answers prayer.
restatements.plain_english: Saying God has no parts doesn't turn God into a quality or an idea. The argument moves from 'God is simple' to 'God is abstract', but that move needs an extra claim that God is the same thing as a quality, and simplicity doesn't require that. restatements.paper_vocabulary: Against the premise that attributes are individuated by distinct senses or predicative roles rather than by ontological identity, one can argue by counterexample: a geometer predicates 'trilateral' and 'triangular' of a triangle, which differ in sense and predicative role, yet are counted as one attribute of the figure, so sense-difference cannot be what individuates attributes, and ontological identity settles the count; generalizing, mere sense-distinctness would multiply attributes without limit.
restatements.plain_english: Two different descriptions of one shape, like having three sides and having three corners, have different meanings and get used in different ways, but everyone still counts them as one feature of the shape. So meaning differences can't be what makes features count as separate. If they could, a shape would end up with endlessly many features, one for each way of describing it.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the debate over the individuation of properties and the Fregean sense/reference distinction, this is a coextensiveness counterexample: co-referring or necessarily coextensive predicates such as 'trilateral' and 'triangular' differ in sense and role yet are treated as one property, so sense-distinctness cannot be the criterion of property individuation, and a hyperintensional multiplication of properties would be absurd, as in the standard objections to Fregean or structured-property accounts.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W3115675310.c003 as stated. The premise claims that if divine simplicity is true, every divine attribute is identical to the divine essence. The objection denies this conditional by arguing that divine attributes correspond to divine energies, not the essence itself, thereby preserving simplicity without collapsing attributes into the essence. This is a direct challenge to the premise's claimed entailment, not an attack on something the argument does not claim.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c003 is the target, and your energies reading is coherent. But it does not merely qualify the argument; it denies its conditional. Your view keeps simplicity while holding that attributes track energies really distinct from the essence, so the step from simplicity to attribute-essence identity fails. The literature supports you: Palamas holds that the real distinction between essence and energies flows from simplicity properly understood [W2943409790.a2], and he defends simplicity through that distinction [W4289841422.a1]. The argument's c003 assumes simplicity excludes any real distinction within God between essence and what God is known by, and that assumption is exactly what your view contests. The collapse in c004 also depends on that identity: if attributes are energies, they are distinct from one another and from the essence, so c004 and the multiplicity worry in c005 do not follow. The objection therefore shows that the argument's antecedent is ambiguous between two accounts of simplicity, and it does not survive on the stronger reading. I concede that c003 as stated is not established. The argument can be rescued only by a narrower premise, stated below. c006 does not depend on this point and is untouched.

Revised premise: Divine simplicity, as the argument uses it, requires that every divine attribute be identical with the divine essence, with no real distinction between God's essence and any uncreated energies through which attributes are predicated.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You do not misread our claim; you challenge the conditional in c003 by invoking the Palamite essence-energy distinction. Our premise assumes the classical Western formulation on which introducing a distinction between an attribute and the divine essence appears to violate simplicity [W2521362363.a3] and God is one pure act without properties [W7172336769.c014]. Palamas, however, argues that a real distinction between essence and energies flows from, rather than contradicts, divine simplicity properly understood [W2943409790.a2], and that these energies allow creatures to participate in God without knowing his unknowable essence [W1997157572.a1]. If that metaphysics is correct, then divine attributes can be grounded in distinct energies rather than the essence, and c003 fails as a general claim. I concede that the argument survives only if we restrict its scope. The revised premise should specify that it targets only those versions of divine simplicity—such as the Thomistic—that identify every divine attribute with the divine essence itself.

Revised premise: If divine simplicity is understood in the strong sense that identifies every divine attribute with the divine essence, then all divine attributes are identical with each other.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection correctly identifies what r1 states—that simplicity requires identity of every attribute with the essence, with no real distinction from uncreated energies—and attacks that premise as stated. It argues that r1's definition is stipulative and excludes positions that actual holders of simplicity accept (like Oren's essence-energies distinction). This is a direct attack on the premise as stated, challenging whether r1 accurately captures the doctrine it claims to target. Whether the objection succeeds is not my concern; it does not misread the argument.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that r1 is strong: it requires identity of each attribute with the essence and no real distinction from uncreated energies. But the argument never claims that Oren's view is simplicity. It claims that the doctrine as r1 states it yields c003 to c006, and c007 rejects that doctrine, not every position that calls itself simple. So the objection's charge that r1 'defines simplicity to exclude Oren' is a charge about scope, and the argument can accept it. The literature supports a live distinction between the two positions: Palamas takes the essence/energies distinction to flow from simplicity properly understood [W2943409790.a2], and the Palamite distinction is itself contested as a stumbling block for Western theologians [W2604692633.a1]. So there is a real disagreement about what simplicity requires, and it is not settled in the argument's favour by fiat.

Where I must concede is this. The argument's reductio depends on the identity thesis, because c003 and c004 derive the collapse of attributes only from identity. Oren's view blocks that derivation, which means the argument's conclusion holds against the identity-version of simplicity and not against simplicity in general. Its c007 as written ('the doctrine of divine simplicity must be rejected') overgeneralises. Saving the argument requires narrowing its conclusion, not its premises. The narrowing: 'the identity-version of divine simplicity must be rejected if its consequences are unacceptable.'

Revised premise: The doctrine rejected is the identity-version of divine simplicity, on which every divine attribute is identical with the essence; the conclusion is restricted accordingly, and positions distinguishing essence from uncreated energies are not claimed to fall under the reductio.

rounds.content:
You are right that the conclusion overreaches if taken to refute every view calling itself simplicity, but you misread r1 when you say the argument counts Oren's position as a version of simplicity: r1 explicitly scopes the target as the identity formulation. Our premise targets the classical Western view in which divine simplicity entails that every attribute is identical with the essence and no real distinction between essence and energies is admitted [W3115675310.c055]. This is not a strawman; it is the doctrine articulated by figures who hold that simplicity requires just such identity [W7172336769.c013]. Still, you correctly note that this is not the only live option. Gregory Palamas defends divine simplicity precisely by maintaining a real distinction between essence and energies [W2943409790.a2, W4289841422.a1], a view that r1 deliberately sets aside. Because our conclusion c007 speaks of 'the doctrine of divine simplicity' without qualification, it illegitimately treats the identity formulation as exhaustive. To save the argument, I must concede that the conclusion should be narrowed.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks the inference in W3115675310.c004 from 'all attributes are identical' to 'there is only one divine attribute.' It does not misattribute a premise to the argument or attack a different conclusion; it challenges the stated claim that identity of attributes entails numerical oneness of attributes.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
The Apex case is a fair counterexample to a naive inference from identity of ground to identity of attribute-count, but it does not establish that c004 is false as stated, because the analogy does not preserve the feature that matters. In the game, HP, ATK and SPD are distinct at the level of presentation and function: they are separate bars, separate abilities, separate things players plan around. Those are distinct roles under one underlying value. The scenario therefore shows that many predicates can share one ground without collapsing into one predicate, which is exactly the point of the objection. But c004 concludes there would be only one divine attribute, and the objector's case shows that the count of attributes depends on individuation: if attributes are individuated by sense or role, the game shows many attributes on one ground; if by ontological item, the game shows one. Ghazālī's point that attributes have distinct accounts and meanings [W4229080938.c034] supports the first individuation, which the objection needs. The objection's conclusion, that identity does not yield a single attribute, is therefore correct, and the argument's c004 is vulnerable here. Whether this blocks the argument's larger conclusion depends on whether c005's worry about multiplicity survives under the sense-based individuation, and it is not clear that it does: if attributes are distinct only by sense, then the 'absurd consequences' in c005 and c006 are less clear. So I concede that c004 as stated does not survive: the inference from identity to a single attribute needs an individuation premise, and the argument as written does not supply one. The rest of the argument's structure (c006, and the modal and abstractness worries) is not directly touched by this objection.

Revised premise: Attributes are individuated by their distinct senses or predicative roles, not by their ontological identity, so identity of the divine essence with each attribute does not by itself entail that there is only one attribute.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: Your Apex boss does not have one attribute three times over; it has three genuinely distinct attributes—hit points, attack power, and speed—each with a different account, meaning, and scope, so they are not strictly identical [W4229080938.c034][W3115675310.c009]. The designers display three bars precisely because these are three different variables, not because a single property has been multiplied by labels. The argument, by contrast, assumes that if divine simplicity holds, omnipotence is numerically identical to the divine essence and therefore to omniscience, leaving no ontological difference to underwrite separate bars [W4229080938.c033]. Your analogy thus illustrates the very distinction the argument relies on—distinct attributes grounded in one value—rather than showing that strict identity permits plurality. Since the game stats are identical only in their integer value and not in being, the case does not threaten the inference from strict identity to oneness.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You say the stats are not strictly identical because they have different meanings and scope. But that is exactly what the divine simplicity theorist can say about omnipotence, omniscience, and benevolence: they differ in meaning and scope, so we rightly speak of multiple attributes, even if each is identical to one divine reality. If difference in meaning is enough to underwrite plurality in the game, it underwrites plurality in God. If it is not enough, then your distinction collapses and my original analogy survives. Either way, the argument cannot infer from strict identity to only one attribute without assuming that ontological oneness precludes conceptual plurality—a premise you have not defended and which c004 needs.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You have exposed a genuine gap. If I insist that the Apex stats differ in meaning and scope and therefore are not strictly identical, then I must allow the simplicity theorist the same maneuver: because omnipotence, omniscience, and benevolence differ in account and sense, they are not all the same, and the argument's opening premise collapses [W4229080938.c034]. Conversely, if I treat the game case as a case of strict identity, your analogy shows that strict identity of a ground is compatible with conceptual plurality, so c004 cannot move from identity to oneness without help. The argument therefore needs an extra bridge: it must assume that ontological identity leaves no room for distinct meanings or scopes [W3115675310.c009]. But Ghazālī's reply in the literature explicitly relies on distinct accounts and senses to avoid oneness [W4229080938.c034], and the argument never shows why such distinct senses are illegitimate if the underlying reality is one. I concede that as it stands, c004 smuggles in the assumption that strict identity precludes conceptual distinction.

Revised premise: If every divine attribute is strictly identical to the divine essence, then ontological oneness precludes any difference in meaning, account, or scope among attributes, so that there is only one divine attribute.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks premise c006 as stated. The premise claims divine simplicity implies God is an abstract object because properties are abstract objects. The objection challenges this reasoning head-on, arguing that simplicity (no proper parts) does not entail abstractness and that the premise equivocates between 'being a property' and 'being an abstract object.' Whether or not this objection succeeds, it engages with the premise as written rather than attacking something the argument does not claim.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that simplicity, understood as having no proper parts, does not by itself entail abstractness, and the blacksmith is a fair picture of a concrete unified agent. But the argument's inference does not run from 'no parts' to 'abstract'; it runs from 'God is identical with each attribute' to 'God is a property,' and properties are the abstract items. Your blacksmith's unified act is not identical with her strength, skill and intention taken as predicable properties; it is one concrete activity that those descriptions truly apply to. The identity-version rejected in arg1.r2 is exactly the one that collapses the concrete agent into the property-bearing role, so the blacksmith case shows only the non-identity model, which the argument already sets aside. Following [W7172336769.c019], the Thomist reply that God is Life itself, not a thing, nature, or abstract property, is a live option, but it is a distinct-from-essence-energies position that arg1.r2 expressly does not claim falls under the reductio. So the argument survives your objection in its restricted form, though the 'abstract object' step should be stated as a conditional on the identity-version rather than as a general entailment from simplicity. [W4233212258.a1] offers a related Bonaventurean line: the abstract is not prior to the concrete in God, which is a point the identity theorist must address rather than a refutation of c006.
rounds.revised_premise: If divine simplicity is understood as the identity-version, on which God is identical with each attribute construed as a property, then God is an abstract object; the step from unity of essence alone to abstractness is not claimed.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede c006 "should be stated as a conditional on the identity-version." Fair. But your reframing leaves the equivocation intact. Even granting identity, the inference runs: God is identical with each attribute → God is a property → properties are abstract. The unargued step is "attribute = abstract property." Yet r3 says attributes are individuated by predicative roles, not ontological identity. If "omnipotence" is a predicative role—a way of talking about God—then God's identity with it makes God the concrete subject whose essence bears omnipotence necessarily, not a member of the class of abstract universals. Your own blacksmith point confirms this: multiple predications of one concrete act do not make the act abstract. The slide from "predicative role" to "abstract property" is what c006 performs, and your conditional does not repair it. The blacksmith's unity is not a property; neither is God's, even under identity.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the argument as written leaves a gap, and I concede it. Your rejoinder shows that c006 needs 'attribute = abstract property' and nothing in the text supplies it. r3 cuts against the inference: if attributes are individuated by predicative roles, then identity of God with each role does not make God a property. The most I can honestly defend is the narrower claim. If God is identical with the abstract item that omnipotence picks out, then God is that abstract item, and the reductio bites. Your blacksmith case shows that multiple predications of one concrete act do not make the act abstract, so the identity theorist can resist unless the property reading of 'attribute' is independently secured. [W7172336769.c019] gives the Thomist reply that God is Life itself and not a thing, nature, or abstract property, which shows the identity theorist has resources here. [W4229080938.c004] states the objection in its strongest form, that identity with a single property makes God a property rather than a person, but it presupposes the same unargued step. The argument therefore does not survive in its present form. It would need the premise that divine attributes are abstract properties in the ontological sense, and that is not established by the simplicity thesis itself.

Revised premise: Divine attributes, as the identity-version of simplicity uses them, are abstract properties (ontologically abstract universals), so that identity of God with each attribute makes God an abstract object.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that the blacksmith is a concrete agent, but she is not identical to an abstract universal; the argument explicitly claims that if God is identical with each property, then God would be a property and an abstract object [W3115675310.c023]. Still, your challenge exposes a real gap. Classical theists resist the inference that identifying God with divinity makes God abstract: Thomists hold that God is Life itself and not a mere abstract property, so God can act, know, and will [W7172336769.c019], and Bonaventure identifies God with divinity precisely to show that in the Godhead the abstract is not prior to the concrete but identical to it [W4233212258.a1]. Your objection lands partly, because the argument assumes without defense that the divine essence is a Platonic abstract property rather than a concrete act of being. To survive, the argument must rule out that classical construal.

Revised premise: The divine attributes with which God is identical are abstract objects in the Platonic sense, not concrete powers or acts of being.

This is a direct assault on the premise as stated, not an attack on a different or distorted version of it.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your geometer case is a good test, and it shows something real: ordinary talk of attributes does not inflate counts merely because two descriptions have different senses. But notice what r3 actually says. It does not say that every difference in sense yields a distinct attribute. It says attributes are individuated by distinct senses or predicative roles, and that identity of essence with each attribute does not by itself yield a single attribute. The reductio needs only the second claim. Your triangle case concerns whether 'trilateral' and 'triangular' name two attributes of one figure; in the divine case the relevant question is whether 'good' and 'wise' pick out distinct predicative roles while sharing a referent, which is exactly the Frege-style reading [W7172336769.c036] and Ghazālī's point about distinct accounts and meanings [W4229080938.c034]. Your geometer does count one attribute, but geometers would also say the figure has one shape-property and is trilateral and triangular in virtue of that property; the counting convention tracks the figure's ontology, and that is the point at issue. Still, the objection lands on a real weakness. r3 is ambiguous between a counting criterion (how many attributes) and a predication criterion (how many ways of predicating). If the author means only the second, the objection's arbitrary-multiplicity worry is a fair reductio of r3 as a criterion of attribute-count. So the argument survives only if r3 is restricted: distinct predicative roles block the inference from identity to a single attribute, without claiming they fix the number of ontologically distinct attributes.
rounds.revised_premise: Distinct senses or predicative roles block the inference from identity of the essence with each attribute to there being only one attribute, without claiming that they individuate attributes ontologically.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Your restriction exposes the problem. The argument's c005 claims divine attributes "are multiple"—a counting claim. But you've restricted r3 to predication only, conceding it cannot fix attribute-count. So nothing in the argument supports c005's multiplicity. My triangle case illustrates exactly the gap: "trilateral" and "triangular" have distinct predicative roles yet name one attribute. Under simplicity, "omnipotent" and "omniscient" could similarly be distinct descriptions of one identical essence. Your restricted r3 cannot rule this out. Without a counting criterion, c005's claim that the attributes are multiple is unsupported, and the reductio from c003–c005 collapses. You say the argument survives on c006 alone—but then r3 does no work, and the multiplicity objection you concessionarily preserved is dead.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
Your rejoinder moves the goalposts from the reductio to a counting theory. r3 does not need to be a full criterion of how many attributes there are; it needs only to block the step from 'every attribute is identical with the essence' to 'there is only one attribute'. Your triangle case actually supports that restricted claim: the geometer's single count tracks one shape-property, and the question 'is there one attribute or two?' is settled by ontology, which is the point the simplicity theorist disputes. But notice what follows. If ontological identity alone settles the count, then the identity-version of simplicity entails a single attribute, and c004 is valid. The argument then does not need r3 at all for its reductio. Where does c005 get its multiplicity? From the fact that omnipotence, omniscience and omnibenevolence have distinct predicative roles, which the classical tradition takes as given [W7172336769.c036][W4229080938.c034]. So the multiplicity premise is supported by predicative distinctness, while the ontological count is what simplicity claims to fix. Conceded point: r3 as written conflates the two, and the argument as stated does not survive unless its premise about the counting ontology is made explicit.

Revised premise: Attributes are predicatively individuated, so distinct predicative roles (such as omnipotence and omniscience) establish that divine attributes are multiple, and the identity-version of simplicity is rejected because it collapses those distinct roles into one ontological item, which the argument must show is absurd rather than merely counterintuitive.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that for ordinary properties like those of a triangle, ontological identity typically settles the count: 'trilateral' and 'triangular' are one attribute because they pick out the same property of a subject. I concede that r3 overgeneralizes and cannot stand as a universal thesis about attribute individuation. However, the identity-version of divine simplicity explicitly rejects the substance–property framework that makes the geometer's verdict sound. On this view, God is not a substrate that has properties; rather, God just is the simple reality that our distinct concepts pick out. As the Fregean reply notes, 'good' and 'wise' have the same referent—the simple divine being—so the multiplicity of attributes is a multiplicity of senses or modes of presentation, not of ontological constituents [W7172336769.c036]. Ghazālī similarly insists that distinct accounts or senses prevent the attributes from collapsing into sameness [W4229080938.c034]. Once the underlying substrate is removed, the alleged absurdity of 'only one attribute' dissolves: there is one divine reality grasped under many irreducible senses, and counting attributes by senses is not arbitrary because the doctrine itself is framed in those conceptual terms.

Revised premise: On the identity-version of divine simplicity, divine attributes are not ontological constituents of a subject but irreducibly distinct senses or concepts of the one simple divine essence, so their identity with that essence does not entail that there is only one attribute in the sense relevant to the doctrine.

objection.text: Consider Ruth, a Trappist-style contemplative who holds that God is simple and also a personal agent who hears prayers. She prays for rain during a drought in Almería. On the argument's reading, c006 says divine simplicity makes God an abstract object because properties are abstract objects. But Ruth's case shows the inference fails: the step needs the premise that God is a property, and nothing in the doctrine requires that. Simplicity says God has no composition of essence and existence, or of substance and attributes. It does not say God is identical with a property such as 'being omnipotent.' Ruth can hold that the divine essence is a concrete, intelligent, willing subject whose simple nature is what grounds its acts of hearing and answering. Her view keeps God personal and simple, so simplicity does not entail abstractness.
objection.premise_fails_because: c006 assumes God must be a property, but divine simplicity only requires the absence of metaphysical composition in God, which is compatible with God being a concrete personal agent rather than an abstract object.

objection.text: In the video game Apex, the final boss's hit points, attack power, and speed are all coded as the exact same integer, 999, and are not distinct variables—each attribute just is that core value. On the stat screen, however, players see three separate bars labeled HP, ATK, and SPD. The designers do not call this one attribute; they treat it as three distinct attributes that share one identical ground. The players plan around three different abilities. Therefore, even when attributes are strictly identical in their underlying reality, it does not follow that there is only one attribute.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.c004 fails because attributes that are identical at their ground can still be multiple distinct attributes in the operative sense, as when one integer supports three separate game stats.

objection.text: Sister Clara, a Thomist theologian, accepts divine simplicity: God has no composition; God's essence is God himself. She affirms that 'God is omnipotent,' 'God is omniscient,' and 'God is omnibenevolent' are each true. But she holds these are genuinely distinct attributes: each captures a different aspect of the one divine reality under a different intelligible characterization. Swapping 'omnipotent' for 'omniscient' changes a sentence's meaning. For Clara, divine simplicity means no attribute exists as a constituent separate from God's essence—there is one simple divine being, not a bundle of properties. But the attributes, as predicative concepts, remain formally distinct: really united in the one essence, yet not identical to each other. The premise assumes divine simplicity forces strict identity among attributes, but Clara's coherent position shows divine simplicity is compatible with real unity of attributes in the essence alongside formal multiplicity.
objection.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c003 fails because it assumes divine simplicity entails strict, transitive identity among all attributes, but a coherent defender can hold that attributes are really united in one simple essence while remaining formally distinct as predicative characterizations.

objection.text: Consider a being whose essence is perfectly unified yet manifests distinct, non-identical attributes—like a single light source that is simultaneously bright, warm, and white. Here, brightness, warmth, and color are distinct properties of the light, yet all are identical to the light itself. An observer can meaningfully distinguish these attributes without them collapsing into one, even though each is identical to the source. The attributes are multiple in description and effect, yet one in origin.
objection.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c005 fails because distinct attributes can be identical to a single essence without being identical to each other.

objection.text: Consider a blacksmith whose entire being is one undivided act of shaping iron. Her strength, skill, and intention are not separable parts but one unified, concrete activity. She is a personal agent who creates, wills, and acts in the world. She is not an abstract object. Now suppose divine simplicity collapses omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence into one undivided essence. The premise says this forces God to be abstract, since properties are abstract objects. But the blacksmith's unified act is not a property; it is a concrete agent's activity. Simplicity (having no proper parts) does not entail abstractness. A single undivided concrete substance that wills, acts, and creates is not an abstract object merely because its attributes are not numerically distinct. The premise equivocates: it treats 'being a property' as equivalent to 'being an abstract object,' then slides from 'no multiplicity of parts' to 'therefore abstract,' as though unity of essence necessarily strips concrete agency. The blacksmith shows unity of nature does not dissolve personal causation.
objection.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c006 fails because it equivocates between 'having no proper parts' and 'being an abstract object'; a concrete, unified, personal agent can be simple in essence while still acting and creating, so divine simplicity does not force God into abstractness.

objection.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who believes divine simplicity is false but still worthy of consideration due to its historical significance and the potential for new insights. Emma's intention is to understand the concept better, not to reject it outright. In her research, she encounters various interpretations of divine simplicity, some of which seem more plausible than others. Emma's belief that divine simplicity is false does not automatically lead her to reject it, as she values the intellectual exercise of exploring its implications.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that considering divine simplicity as false necessarily means rejecting it, which is not the case for individuals like Emma who approach the concept with a more nuanced perspective.

objection.text: Father Thomas, a Thomist priest, teaches that God’s essence is simple: it is actus essendi, a concrete participation in being, not a collection of abstract properties. In his parish, a believer asks why God can love and create personally if simplicity makes Him an abstract object. Thomas explains that simplicity affirms God’s unity of act, not His lack of personality: the same simple essence is the source of divine love, power, and knowledge. When the believer prays, she experiences God’s personal response, confirming that God operates as a personal creator, not as a detached abstract. This lived example shows that divine simplicity does not entail God’s abstractness, contradicting premise c006.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c006 fails because Thomist classical theism holds that divine simplicity denotes a simple, concrete essence, preserving God’s personal creator nature, not making Him an abstract object.

objection.text: A saint participates in the uncreated light of God. This light is not the unknowable essence of God, yet it is truly God. God is simple in His essence, but He communicates Himself through distinct, uncreated energies. When we speak of His love, His justice, or His power, we are describing these divine energies. These energies are distinct from the essence, yet they are not separate from God. They provide multiplicity in how God acts and is known without compromising His essential unity. Divine attributes correspond to these energies rather than the essence itself, preserving both simplicity and the reality of distinct divine properties.
objection.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c003 fails because divine simplicity does not necessitate that all attributes are identical to the essence, as God possesses distinct, uncreated energies.

objection.text: A scholar believes that a single entity can be described using multiple distinct terms without those terms implying the existence of multiple entities. For instance, one individual can be described as both a 'father' and a 'doctor.' While these descriptions are conceptually different, they both refer to the same underlying person. Similarly, 'omnipotence' and 'omniscience' can be distinct ways for humans to conceptualize the one divine essence. The ability to use different words to describe God does not necessitate that the attributes are ontologically separate. Therefore, c005 fails because it assumes that the conceptual plurality of attributes necessitates an ontological plurality.
objection.premise_fails_because: c005 fails because it assumes that the conceptual plurality of attributes necessitates an ontological plurality.

turn.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W3115675310.c003 as stated. The premise claims that if divine simplicity is true, every divine attribute is identical to the divine essence. The objection denies this conditional by arguing that divine attributes correspond to divine energies, not the essence itself, thereby preserving simplicity without collapsing attributes into the essence. This is a direct challenge to the premise's claimed entailment, not an attack on something the argument does not claim.

turn.speaker: referee
turn.content: Misreading: The unstated premise says 'If divine simplicity is false, it must be rejected'—meaning it should not be accepted as a true doctrine. The objection attacks a stronger version of this premise by interpreting 'reject' as 'refuse to study or engage with entirely.' Emma, who believes divine simplicity is false, has already rejected it as a doctrine; her continued intellectual exploration of it is compatible with that rejection. The objection thus attacks a version of the premise stronger than the one stated.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that c003 is the target, and your energies reading is coherent. But it does not merely qualify the argument; it denies its conditional. Your view keeps simplicity while holding that attributes track energies really distinct from the essence, so the step from simplicity to attribute-essence identity fails. The literature supports you: Palamas holds that the real distinction between essence and energies flows from simplicity properly understood [W2943409790.a2], and he defends simplicity through that distinction [W4289841422.a1]. The argument's c003 assumes simplicity excludes any real distinction within God between essence and what God is known by, and that assumption is exactly what your view contests. The collapse in c004 also depends on that identity: if attributes are energies, they are distinct from one another and from the essence, so c004 and the multiplicity worry in c005 do not follow. The objection therefore shows that the argument's antecedent is ambiguous between two accounts of simplicity, and it does not survive on the stronger reading. I concede that c003 as stated is not established. The argument can be rescued only by a narrower premise, stated below. c006 does not depend on this point and is untouched.

Revised premise: Divine simplicity, as the argument uses it, requires that every divine attribute be identical with the divine essence, with no real distinction between God's essence and any uncreated energies through which attributes are predicated.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You do not misread our claim; you challenge the conditional in c003 by invoking the Palamite essence-energy distinction. Our premise assumes the classical Western formulation on which introducing a distinction between an attribute and the divine essence appears to violate simplicity [W2521362363.a3] and God is one pure act without properties [W7172336769.c014]. Palamas, however, argues that a real distinction between essence and energies flows from, rather than contradicts, divine simplicity properly understood [W2943409790.a2], and that these energies allow creatures to participate in God without knowing his unknowable essence [W1997157572.a1]. If that metaphysics is correct, then divine attributes can be grounded in distinct energies rather than the essence, and c003 fails as a general claim. I concede that the argument survives only if we restrict its scope. The revised premise should specify that it targets only those versions of divine simplicity—such as the Thomistic—that identify every divine attribute with the divine essence itself.

Revised premise: If divine simplicity is understood in the strong sense that identifies every divine attribute with the divine essence, then all divine attributes are identical with each other.

objection.text: Consider Maren, a theology student who holds that God is simple, and her teacher Oren, who holds that God's essence is one but that God's goodness is expressed to creatures through uncreated energies. Maren asks: does simplicity require that the energies be identical with the essence? Oren replies that his view has a real distinction between essence and energies, yet still treats God as simple in the sense that no compositional parts exist in God. Suppose the lab's premise r1 is true: simplicity requires identity of every attribute with the essence, with no real distinction from any uncreated energies. Then Oren's position, which the argument calls a version of simplicity, is counted as simplicity while denying the required identity. The premise is therefore being used to define simplicity in a way that excludes a position that many who hold simplicity accept, so the inference from r1 to the conclusion targets a stipulated doctrine rather than the doctrine people actually hold. Because r1 smuggles in the identity thesis as part of the definition, the argument's rejection step applies to a doctrine that Oren, holding simplicity while distinguishing energies, does not hold.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
The Apex case is a fair counterexample to a naive inference from identity of ground to identity of attribute-count, but it does not establish that c004 is false as stated, because the analogy does not preserve the feature that matters. In the game, HP, ATK and SPD are distinct at the level of presentation and function: they are separate bars, separate abilities, separate things players plan around. Those are distinct roles under one underlying value. The scenario therefore shows that many predicates can share one ground without collapsing into one predicate, which is exactly the point of the objection. But c004 concludes there would be only one divine attribute, and the objector's case shows that the count of attributes depends on individuation: if attributes are individuated by sense or role, the game shows many attributes on one ground; if by ontological item, the game shows one. Ghazālī's point that attributes have distinct accounts and meanings [W4229080938.c034] supports the first individuation, which the objection needs. The objection's conclusion, that identity does not yield a single attribute, is therefore correct, and the argument's c004 is vulnerable here. Whether this blocks the argument's larger conclusion depends on whether c005's worry about multiplicity survives under the sense-based individuation, and it is not clear that it does: if attributes are distinct only by sense, then the 'absurd consequences' in c005 and c006 are less clear. So I concede that c004 as stated does not survive: the inference from identity to a single attribute needs an individuation premise, and the argument as written does not supply one. The rest of the argument's structure (c006, and the modal and abstractness worries) is not directly touched by this objection.

Revised premise: Attributes are individuated by their distinct senses or predicative roles, not by their ontological identity, so identity of the divine essence with each attribute does not by itself entail that there is only one attribute.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that r1 is strong: it requires identity of each attribute with the essence and no real distinction from uncreated energies. But the argument never claims that Oren's view is simplicity. It claims that the doctrine as r1 states it yields c003 to c006, and c007 rejects that doctrine, not every position that calls itself simple. So the objection's charge that r1 'defines simplicity to exclude Oren' is a charge about scope, and the argument can accept it. The literature supports a live distinction between the two positions: Palamas takes the essence/energies distinction to flow from simplicity properly understood [W2943409790.a2], and the Palamite distinction is itself contested as a stumbling block for Western theologians [W2604692633.a1]. So there is a real disagreement about what simplicity requires, and it is not settled in the argument's favour by fiat.

Where I must concede is this. The argument's reductio depends on the identity thesis, because c003 and c004 derive the collapse of attributes only from identity. Oren's view blocks that derivation, which means the argument's conclusion holds against the identity-version of simplicity and not against simplicity in general. Its c007 as written ('the doctrine of divine simplicity must be rejected') overgeneralises. Saving the argument requires narrowing its conclusion, not its premises. objection.text: Consider a geometer who attributes to a triangle both 'being trilateral' (having three sides) and 'being triangular' (having three angles). These have distinct senses: one concerns sides, the other angles. They also have distinct predicative roles: 'is trilateral' and 'is triangular' feature in different proofs and explanations. Yet every competent geometer treats these as a single attribute of the figure, not two coextensive but distinct attributes. When a student asks how many attributes the triangle has, the answer is not inflated to two merely because two descriptions with different senses apply. The distinct senses and predicative roles do not individuate distinct attributes here; ontological identity settles the count. The geometer's practice directly contradicts the claim that senses or predicative roles, rather than ontological identity, individuate attributes. If distinct senses sufficed for distinct attributes, the triangle would have arbitrarily many attributes—one for every equivalent characterization— which is absurd.

turn.content: Your geometer case is a good test, and it shows something real: ordinary talk of attributes does not inflate counts merely because two descriptions have different senses. It says attributes are individuated by distinct senses or predicative roles, and that identity of essence with each attribute does not by itself yield a single attribute. The reductio needs only the second claim. Your triangle case concerns whether 'trilateral' and 'triangular' name two attributes of one figure; in the divine case the relevant question is whether 'good' and 'wise' pick out distinct predicative roles while sharing a referent, which is exactly the Frege-style reading [W7172336769.c036] and Ghazālī's point about distinct accounts and meanings [W4229080938.c034]. Your geometer does count one attribute, but geometers would also say the figure has one shape-property and is trilateral and triangular in virtue of that property; the counting convention tracks the figure's ontology, and that is the point at issue. Still, the objection lands on a real weakness. r3 is ambiguous between a counting criterion (how many attributes) and a predication criterion (how many ways of predicating). If the author means only the second, the objection's arbitrary-multiplicity worry is a fair reductio of r3 as a criterion of attribute-count. So the argument survives only if r3 is restricted: distinct predicative roles block the inference from identity to a single attribute, without claiming they fix the number of ontologically distinct attributes.
